name: Bus Fleets
description: Iran’s bus fleets raise distinct questions about urban air quality, vehicle maintenance, and intercity passenger safety. Research on Tehran’s diesel buses illustrates why modernization depends on fuel and maintenance systems as well as vehicles.

seo.title: Bus Fleets in Iran: Maintenance, Emissions and Safety
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to bus modernization in Iran, distinguishing Tehran’s diesel retrofit research from intercity safety and current fleet evidence.

content.heading: Modernization beyond buying buses
content.content:
A World Bank assessment published in June 2019 examined retrofitting Tehran’s ageing diesel buses with diesel particulate filters: equipment that captures particles from exhaust. Its central lesson was that vehicles and fuel must be treated together. Suitable low-sulfur diesel, maintenance, and operating conditions influence whether filters deliver their intended benefits. The report also identified advantages in targeting a centrally fueled and maintained urban fleet, where training and oversight can be organized more readily. [s1]

This was an assessment of retrofit options, including modeled future costs and benefits. Its projections do not establish that the proposed program was subsequently completed. Nor does its historical fleet baseline establish how many buses were operating at the editorial cutoff. The distinction matters: an economic case for modernization is evidence about a proposed intervention, rather than an audited record of implementation. [s1]

content.heading: Intercity safety requires separate evidence
content.content:
Urban emissions research cannot describe every problem facing intercity coaches. Reporting on an October 2025 crash on the Damavand–Firouzkouh road, northeast of Tehran, described a bus traveling from Qazvin toward Mazandaran. The report attributed an initial suggestion of driver fatigue to the road police chief. That was a preliminary account, not a final investigation establishing the cause. [s2]

The case illustrates why a fleet account must distinguish vehicle condition, driver working conditions, and the circumstances of a particular journey. A crash report alone cannot establish the mechanical condition of Iran’s national fleet or demonstrate that ageing vehicles caused an individual collision. Conversely, evidence about cleaner exhaust does not establish better crash performance. These are separate outcomes requiring separate verification. [s1][s2]

name: Intercity Transport
description: Intercity road transport connects passenger journeys with a wider system of road information and incident management. Reporting from June 2025 also shows how international coach services became an alternative when flights to Iran were disrupted.

seo.title: Intercity Road Transport in Iran: Journeys and Disruption
seo.description: Explore documented aspects of Iran’s intercity road travel, including road information and the role of international coaches during flight disruption.

content.heading: The information behind a journey
content.content: An institutional presentation delivered on behalf of Iran’s Road Maintenance and Transportation Organization describes the National Road Management Center’s work on weather, road closures, work zones, and incidents. It identifies the 141 information service among the channels used to communicate road conditions. This documents an information function supporting road journeys; it is not a passenger timetable or evidence that a particular departure is operating. The presentation is historical, and its descriptions should not be read as a verification of current service availability. [s1]

content.heading: Coaches when flights stop
content.content:
Reporting from Istanbul in June 2025 provides a concrete example of road transport adapting to disruption. Following airspace closures during the Israel–Iran conflict, travelers who had expected to fly to Iran instead boarded coaches in Istanbul. The National interviewed drivers, travel managers, and passengers, including people whose original journeys had begun outside Turkey. [s2]

The account reveals more than a substitution between vehicles. Passengers described interrupted itineraries, difficulty contacting family, and uncertainty about returning. Coach travel linked an international arrival point to an overland route home, while imposing a much longer journey. These interviews document experiences during a specific crisis; they do not measure normal national demand or establish a permanent route schedule. [s2]

For understanding intercity transport, the useful distinction is between the existence of a road connection and the availability of a usable passenger service. The reported departures establish that coaches operated in that episode. They do not establish present fares, border procedures, ticket availability, or journey times. Those details require dated operator and border-authority evidence before they can support a current travel account. [s2]

name: Traffic Management Systems
description: Iranian traffic-management documentation describes systems for observing road conditions, coordinating incident information, and informing travelers. Research in Tehran separately demonstrates how transport data can be combined to estimate travel demand.

seo.title: Traffic Management Systems in Iran: Monitoring and Analysis
seo.description: Understand documented road-monitoring functions in Iran and Tehran research using transport data, with clear limits on claims about deployment and performance.

content.heading: From observation to information
content.content: A presentation delivered on behalf of Iran’s Road Maintenance and Transportation Organization describes a National Road Management Center workflow linking information collection, analysis, incident coordination, and public announcements. Its equipment inventory includes cameras, traffic counters, weather systems, speed enforcement, and weighing vehicles in motion. These perform different functions: observing a road is distinct from enforcing a rule or dispatching assistance. The presentation documents institutional descriptions rather than independently audited performance. [s1]

content.title: A documented road-information workflow
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Road observations and reports"] -->|"Supply information"| B["National Road Management Center"]
  B -->|"Analyze and register events"| C["Incident information"]
  C -->|"Share for coordination"| D["Responsible response agencies"]
  C -->|"Support public announcements"| E["Traveler information channels"]
```
content.summary: The arrows represent information handling and coordination described in the historical presentation. They do not establish command authority or guaranteed response times.

content.heading: Understanding where trips begin and end
content.content:
Traffic observations can also support planning research. A 2021 study of Tehran combined automatic number plate recognition, public-transport smart-card records, intersection loop-detector counts, navigation GPS data, and characteristics of urban zones. Its objective was to estimate an origin–destination matrix: a representation of trips between starting and ending areas. [s2]

These inputs describe different aspects of movement. A count at an intersection does not by itself reveal a complete journey, while a recorded location does not explain a traveler’s purpose. The researchers therefore combined sources and evaluated estimated matrices against a reference matrix from comprehensive transportation studies. Their comparison considered both numerical error and the structure of the estimated travel pattern. [s2]

This distinction between observation and inference is essential. The study demonstrates a research method applied to Tehran data; it does not establish that its model was deployed across the city or that it reduced congestion. Nor does good performance in the reported case establish equivalent performance elsewhere in Iran. A current account of traffic management needs operational evidence alongside research results. [s2]
